Kanjidon vs WaniKani 2026: Which Kanji App Fits You?

Kanjidon Team · Feb 3, 2026

Kanjidon and WaniKani both use scheduled review, but they solve different study problems. WaniKani provides a fixed web curriculum built around its component mnemonics, kanji and vocabulary. Kanjidon provides a mobile, JLPT-oriented collection with varied quiz formats. The useful question is not which logo wins; it is which workflow matches the way you want to study.

Quick Comparison

AreaKanjidonWaniKani
Primary focusKana, kanji and vocabulary organised around JLPT studyStructured kanji and vocabulary curriculum
Learning orderChoose a JLPT-focused path and review available materialProgress through 60 levels; content unlocks through reviews
Memory supportSpaced reviews, cards and contextual study materialStaff-written component, meaning and reading mnemonics with SRS
Practice style16 quiz types, including recognition, listening, writing and speaking-related formatsTyped meaning and reading reviews within a consistent lesson system
Free accessKana and N5 path plus 10 welcome packs; Premium expands accessLevels 1–3 free; subscription needed from Level 4
Paid accessPremium; price depends on store and regionPaid subscription options; confirm current plans on the official pricing page

The Main Difference Is Control

WaniKani intentionally controls sequence. Its teaching components, called radicals inside WaniKani, though they are not always traditional dictionary radicals, unlock kanji, and learned kanji unlock vocabulary. The official documentation says content cannot be skipped. This gives the curriculum a coherent internal language, but it can feel slow if you already know material or need a specific JLPT subset soon.

Kanjidon is organised around kana and JLPT levels rather than WaniKani’s proprietary 60-level sequence. Its library contains more than 6,000 kanji and vocabulary cards in total, and its 16 quiz formats can test different aspects of an item. That flexibility still requires judgment: a handwriting or listening exercise does not replace grammar, extensive reading or conversation.

Mnemonics and Components

WaniKani’s curriculum is designed around hand-written mnemonic stories that connect its named components to a kanji meaning and selected reading. This is the heart of the product, not an optional extra. It works best when you are willing to learn WaniKani’s component names and follow its order.

Kanjidon also provides visual and contextual support, but its differentiator is broader practice and collection rather than one required mnemonic vocabulary. In either app, treat a mnemonic as a retrieval cue, not as the historical origin of a character.

Review and Exercise Style

WaniKani asks for typed meanings and readings and moves items through its SRS stages. Kanjidon combines scheduled review with multiple quiz modes, including recognition, drawing, dictation and shadowing-related activities where supported. More formats are useful only when they serve your goal; a learner focused on fast reading may not need every production exercise.

Free Access, Price and Connectivity

WaniKani’s first three levels are free. Paid plans and terms can change, so check its official pricing page before purchasing. Its support documentation also states that an internet connection is required and there is no offline mode.

Kanjidon offers a free kana and N5 path and 10 welcome packs, with Premium expanding the available content and features. It contains no advertising. Some cached study flows can remain usable without a connection, while account, social and other network-dependent features cannot; do not assume that every screen works offline.

Choose WaniKani If

  • You want a curriculum that decides the order for you.
  • You enjoy narrative mnemonics and are happy to learn the system’s component names.
  • Typed meaning and reading reviews are the practice style you want.
  • A web-first, always-online workflow fits your routine.

Choose Kanjidon If

  • You want study organised by kana and JLPT levels.
  • Collectible cards and varied quiz formats help you return consistently.
  • You want recognition, listening, handwriting and speaking-related practice in one mobile app.
  • You prefer to sample a free N5 path before deciding on Premium.

A Fair Test

Try the free portion of each with the same modest daily target. After one or two weeks, compare three things: how many reviews you complete, whether you can read the items outside the app, and whether the workflow fits your available time. The most suitable system is the one you can sustain without mistaking in-app familiarity for Japanese ability.
